text: $ FairRate Audit Home How it works POS services Cost simulator Resources About FAQ Contact Search Free audit About Run by someone who's actually done the switch. Hi, I'm Mike. I'm a business analyst by trade — requirements, process improvement, finding the waste in how things actually work — and I've spent my career inside Canadian retail and logistics. It started in a warehouse office — keeping shipments moving on time and digging into carrier data to build a better process for prioritizing trailer loads. Then a help desk supporting POS systems store by store: hardware upgrades, PCI compliance work, the unglamorous stuff that keeps the tills running. Then four years as a business analyst for purchasing and merchandising — ERP master data, assortment planning, forecast and replenishment, EDI — the systems behind every transaction. For the past two years I've been with a hotel chain — hotels, bars, and retail shops — which took my sector knowledge beyond pure retail into hospitality: food-and-beverage operations and guest-facing systems that can't go down in the middle of service. Before that I was the senior POS specialist for a national retail chain — rolling out a new POS platform and hardware to more than 100 stores across the country, managing the application and hardware vendors to scope and budget, and running the escalation path for stores and district managers. New store openings, renovations, moves, closures: every piece of IT in the store was my checklist. Before that I ran in-store IT infrastructure at one of Canada's largest retailers — three teams, a $15M+ annual budget, and the full lifecycle of everything a store runs on: POS, self-checkouts, pinpads, printers, servers, UPS. My teams replaced 5,900+ pinpads across hundreds of stores and shipped two major POS upgrades. Along the way I personally led four major payment-processor migrations , so when I say I'll project-manage your switch, I'm not working from someone else's playbook. Full processor replacement across live retail stores Processor migration bundled with a complete new POS rollout across the chain Mid-operation processor switch — cutover without stopping the business Greenfield processor setup, integrated with the retailer's existing POS That's the whole reason FairRate Audit exists. Most fee consultants can read a statement. Very few have actually stood in a store during a processor cutover and kept the tills running. When I recommend a switch, I'm not guessing how it goes — I've lived the before and after, four times over. Based in the Toronto area, working with small businesses across Canada — and vendor-independent: Mike works for the business being audited, not for any processor. His specialty beyond payments is retail systems themselves — POS hardware and software, integrations, and inventory — which is why FairRate Audit also offers POS services as a follow-on to the audit. text: $ FairRate Audit Home How it works POS services Cost simulator Resources About FAQ Contact Search Free audit Home › Annual fee report Annual report · 2026 edition The state of small-business processing fees. Once a year we publish what the numbers actually say about card processing costs — what we found in published research, what we're learning from real statements, and exactly how we compute everything. No cherry-picking. Key findings Year-one edition — compiled from published sources This first edition doesn't yet have our own dataset behind it, so we say that up front: everything below comes from published sources, not from our client audits. We'll add our own numbers when the sample is big enough to be honest about. Average effective rate, Visa/Mastercard, 2025 2.36% The Merchants Payments Coalition put the 2025 average Visa/Mastercard effective rate at 2.36% — the headline number for what "average" processing costs look like across the board. Source: Merchants Payments Coalition, via KoronaPOS — Understanding merchant statements . A worked restaurant example 2.07% KoronaPOS's worked example walks a restaurant through its own statement math and lands at 2.07%. Useful as an illustration of how the calculation works — not a benchmark for what your business should pay. Source: KoronaPOS — Understanding merchant statements . Illustrative example, not a target rate. The interchange settlement −0.10 pts, 1.25% cap — preliminary In April 2026 the interchange settlement received preliminary court approval: roughly a 0.10-percentage-point cut with a 1.25% cap on covered interchange. Preliminary means exactly that — not final, not yet in your statement, and the details can still move. Status: preliminary approval only. We'll update this finding if and when it becomes final. To be published when our data supports it These are the sections we're building toward. They'll appear here — and in the annual PDF — only once we have enough real submissions to back them honestly. We publish medians with sample sizes, never cherry-picked figures. Effective rates by sector Retail, restaurants, quick-service, hotels, grocery, salons — what comparable businesses actually pay, reported anonymously through our transparency wall . Each cell needs enough reports to be statistically honest before it goes live. Effective rates by processor Same data, cut by processor rather than sector. Published only when individual processors have enough independent reports that the median can't be skewed by a handful of unusual accounts. Fee-trend analysis Are rates actually moving year over year, or just reshuffling between line items? This needs multiple years of comparable data — it starts appearing in the 2027 edition at the earliest. Our sample-size rule: public aggregates appear only where we have enough independent reports that the median is meaningful — at minimum, cells with fewer than three reports stay hidden, and bigger claims need bigger samples. A figure without a sample size next to it is a rumor, not data. Methodology: how the audit reads a statement The same method behind our audits is the method behind this report. No magic — just careful reading. Pull total fees and total volume. We take every fee on the statement — interchange, assessment, processor markup, monthly fees, terminal fees, the lot — and divide by total card volume for the period. That's the effective rate : the single number that tells you what you're really paying. Separate the three cost layers. Interchange (goes to the card-issuing banks), card-brand assessments (Visa/Mastercard/Amex), and processor markup (the part your processor actually controls). You can't negotiate interchange — it's set by the card brands — but the markup is where overcharges hide. Check the markup against pricing tier. We compare what the processor kept against published interchange-plus and flat-rate pricing for your sector and volume band, to see whether the markup is competitive or padded. Scan for junk fees. Line items that have no card-brand equivalent and add no value — "statement fees," "PCI non-compliance fees" charged to compliant merchants, duplicated monthly charges. These come out one by one. Verify against multiple months. Three to six months of statements, so seasonal swings and one-off spikes don't skew the picture. The baseline we negotiate from is a documented average, not a lucky month. Document the savings formula. The audit fee is computed from documented monthly savings — baseline effective rate × current volume minus actual fees, spelled out as a written exhibit — so every number in this report, and in our client work, traces back to real statements. desc: Frequently asked questions about the FairRate Audit payment processing audit: switching, statements, how savings are measured, data privacy, and fees.
text: $ FairRate Audit Home How it works POS services Cost simulator Resources About FAQ Contact Search Free audit Questions Fair questions, straight answers. Do I have to switch processors? No. Every audit considers two plays: renegotiating with your current processor (same terminals, no disruption) and switching to better pricing (usually bigger savings, with the migration project-managed for you). You choose — some clients never switch. What statements do you need? Three to six months of recent merchant processing statements, in PDF or whatever format your processor gives you. That's enough to compute your true effective rate and spot mispricing. How exactly are "savings" measured? First we compute your baseline effective rate (total fees ÷ total volume over your statements). Each month after the fix, savings = (baseline rate × that month's volume) − your actual fees. The formula is written into your agreement as an exhibit, so there's never a debate about what counts. What does it cost if no savings are found? Nothing. The audit is free, and if we can't document real savings you owe us nothing. Our fee only exists when savings exist: 50% of documented monthly savings, for a fixed term agreed in writing before any work starts. How long does the savings share last? A fixed term — usually 24 months — agreed in your contract before work begins. After the term ends, you keep 100% of the savings. We also offer an optional annual re-audit to keep rate creep from eating your gains. Is my data private? Yes. Your statements contain sensitive business and banking details, and we treat them that way: confidential handling, no sharing with third parties, and data-handling practices aligned with Canada's PIPEDA privacy law. See our privacy policy . Do you get paid by processors too? Our primary fee comes from you, the client — that's what keeps us independent. If a processor referral bonus is ever part of a recommendation we make, it is disclosed to you in writing before you sign anything. No hidden payments. What if my volume drops or I close? The fee floats on your actual monthly savings — if a slow month produces no savings, there's no fee that month. The agreement spells out what happens if you change processors or close, and there's no early-termination fee designed to trap you. Who is this not for? Very low card volumes (under ~$10,000/month) rarely produce enough savings to be worth anyone's time — we'll tell you that honestly in the audit. Businesses already on well-priced interchange-plus plans usually have little to gain, and we'll say so. Do you also work on POS systems? Yes — it's the natural follow-on. A POS health check reviews your terminals, software, integrations, and inventory data, then we quote project-priced work: terminal refresh advisory, POS software migration, integrations (POS ↔ accounting, POS ↔ ecommerce, loyalty, gift cards), and inventory setup and cleanup. Advisory and sourcing only — we don't sell or stock hardware. See POS services for details. Still curious? Ask us directly — or just send the statements and see the numbers. text: $ FairRate Audit Home How it works POS services Cost simulator Resources About FAQ Contact Search Free audit Home › How we get paid Radical disclosure Here's exactly how we make money. Most "free audit" services in this industry are quietly paid by the processors they recommend. We think you should know every dollar that touches your account — so this page is the full, written record of who pays us and how. How we get paid today Our revenue comes from one place: a share of the savings we document for you. The audit is free. The analysis is free. We only get paid if we find real, documented savings — and then our fee is 50% of the documented monthly savings, paid over 24–36 months. The written exhibit Every service agreement carries the savings formula as a written exhibit, so the math is never a matter of opinion: Documented monthly savings = (baseline effective rate × current monthly volume) − actual monthly fees paid The baseline effective rate is computed from your 3–6 months of pre-audit statements. "Actual monthly fees paid" comes straight from your processor statements during the fee period. Our fee is 50% of that documented monthly savings figure. Nothing found = nothing owed. If the audit shows your rates are already competitive, you get a clean bill of health and pay us zero. And one more structural guarantee: We never hold your money. You pay your processor directly, as you always have. You pay our audit fee separately. We never touch, hold, or route your merchant funds. Processor referral fees — the honest status As of 2026-09-28, we take NO referral or bounty fees from any processor. Not from Moneris, not from Stripe, not from anyone — no referral fees, no bounties, no "partner" payouts, no volume bonuses. Nothing. The 50% shared-savings fee from you is our entire processing-related revenue right now. We're saying this in writing, on a dated page, because the industry norm is the opposite: plenty of "free audit" firms are paid by processors for every account they steer over. If that ever becomes true of us, this page is where you'll read about it first — see below. Our written firewall policy A promise is cheap. A mechanism is credible. Here's the mechanism that keeps our recommendations honest, whether or not referral fees ever exist: The alignment Our fee is a percentage of your savings Audit recommendations are driven only by documented savings. Because our fee is a percentage of those savings, recommending a worse deal just to chase a bounty would shrink our own fee — the math fights against any incentive to steer you wrong. The structure No quotas, no exclusivity We carry no volume quotas with any processor and no exclusivity arrangements that could compromise recommendations. We're free to recommend whoever's numbers are best — including "stay where you are and renegotiate." This firewall is part of every service agreement we sign, not just a line on this page. What goes into your agreement Every service agreement carries this disclosure language verbatim. Nothing buried, nothing in fine print: Processor compensation disclosure. If we ever receive compensation from a processor related to your account — referral fees, bounties, bonuses, or any other payment — it will be disclosed here in writing before you sign anything, including the amount and the processor paying it. You will never be asked to sign an agreement with undisclosed processor compensation attached to your account. What changes if bounties ever exist Someday a processor may offer us a referral fee, and we may take it. If that day comes, here's the standing policy, in advance, so there's no ambiguity later: The exact amounts will be published per processor on this page — before the first one is taken, not after. Your individual agreement will carry the disclosure paragraph above, naming the processor and the amount. The firewall policy doesn't move: recommendations stay driven by documented savings, and our percentage-of-savings fee keeps the alignment. If a processor relationship ever conflicts with a client's best interest, the client's interest wins — that's the whole point of the firewall, and it's in writing. It is not compliance advice, it doesn't cover assessment types or detailed rules, and PCI requirements change. For the actual requirements that apply to you, check current official requirements here: PCI Security Standards Council — the official source. The core principle One sentence that explains 90% of PCI scope decisions. If card data passes through a system, that system is in scope. If card data never touches it, it generally isn't. That's the whole game: every cable, Wi-Fi hop, and software integration that carries (or could carry) card numbers drags the systems on both ends into your compliance obligations. Design your setup so card data travels the shortest possible path — ideally, it never leaves the payment terminal at all. Think of it like plumbing: you don't waterproof the whole house, you keep the water in the pipes. The terminal is the pipe. Everything else should stay dry. The three architectures Every card-present setup is some version of one of these. Smallest scope 1. Standalone terminal The terminal sits on the counter, connected directly to the processor. The cashier keys in (or the customer sees) the amount, the card is tapped or inserted, and the receipt prints from the terminal. Card data never touches your POS, your PC, or your network beyond carrying the terminal's own encrypted traffic. Because nothing else in your business ever sees card data, your POS, back-office computers, and other systems are largely out of scope. This is the simplest architecture to secure and to assess — which is why it's the right choice for many small businesses that don't need deep POS integration. Customer card tap / insert / swipe Standalone terminal card data stays here Processor moves the money POS & back-office PC — outside the card-data path ← card data path Small scope, if done right 2. Semi-integrated / P2PE terminal Here the terminal connects to your POS so the sale amount flows automatically (no re-keying), but card data still never touches the POS . The terminal encrypts the card data the instant it's read and sends it straight to the processor; the POS only ever sees non-sensitive references like approval codes and totals. "P2PE-validated" at a high level: P2PE stands for point-to-point encryption. A P2PE-validated solution is one where an independent assessor has verified that card data is encrypted inside the terminal and stays encrypted until it reaches the processor — with validated controls around the devices and decryption environment. In plain terms: it's a setup someone qualified has checked actually keeps card data out of your systems, rather than a vendor merely claiming it does. Done properly, the POS stays largely out of scope — you get the convenience of integration without dragging your whole network into scope. Done improperly (card data readable anywhere along the path), it quietly becomes architecture #3. Largest scope 3. Card data passing through the POS In this architecture, card data flows through the POS software or the PC it runs on — for example, a card reader plugged into the POS computer that sends unencrypted card data through the POS application to the processor. The POS is now in scope — and so is everything connected to it: the PC, the network it sits on, and potentially the back-office systems it talks to. Your compliance obligations grow substantially, and so does your breach risk: card data sitting in more places means more places it can be stolen from. If your setup works this way and you didn't deliberately choose it, that's worth a conversation with your vendors about moving to architecture #1 or #2. The takeaway Card data through the POS → the POS is in scope. Standalone terminal, or an appropriately semi-integrated / P2PE-validated device → the POS is largely out of scope. When a vendor proposes a setup, ask one question: "Show me exactly where the card data travels." Then check the current official requirements at the PCI Security Standards Council . Seven common scope-creep mistakes Ways businesses accidentally pull more systems into scope than they needed to. Keying card numbers into the POS "just this once" Typing a card number into the POS for a phone order or a failed terminal puts card data into a system that wasn't designed to hold it. Use your processor's virtual terminal or a proper card-not-present flow instead — and never as a routine workaround. Storing card numbers in notes, spreadsheets, or booking fields A card number in a booking note, a spreadsheet of "regulars," or an email thread is card data sitting in systems with none of the right protections. Tokenize (store a token, not the number) or don't store it at all. Putting the terminal on the same network as everything else A flat network where the terminal, the POS, the back-office PC, and guest Wi-Fi all mingle means card-data traffic shares space with everything. Segment the payment traffic away from the rest. Letting guest Wi-Fi touch business systems Guest devices on the same network as terminals or the POS is a scope and security problem at once. Guest Wi-Fi must be isolated — no path to payment, POS, or PMS systems. Assuming "the cloud handles it" Cloud POS doesn't automatically mean small scope. POS end-of-life assessment Every terminal on your counter has a retirement date — set by the manufacturer, not by you. We find it before it finds you. What it means End of life, in plain terms When a manufacturer declares a terminal or POS component end-of-life, three things stop: security patches , spare parts , and vendor support . The device doesn't stop working that day — it stops getting safer. For a small business, that means the machine reading your customers' card data is frozen in time while fraud techniques keep moving — and when it breaks, the fix is a scramble instead of a phone call. Costs Replacing on purpose vs. replacing in a panic A planned replacement is priced, scheduled, and installed on a quiet day. Staying past end-of-life trades that for three real costs: downtime risk (no working terminal means no card sales, for as long as a replacement takes to arrive), emergency-replacement premiums (rush orders and expedited shipping cost more than the same hardware bought calmly), and PCI exposure (unpatched payment devices are a compliance liability — a breach is the most expensive "saving" there is). The assessment puts numbers on both sides, so the call is a business decision instead of a gamble. Draft — Mike to confirm What can keep running past end-of-life — and what can't This guidance is a working draft. Mike confirms the final call for your specific equipment before anything is acted on. The general principle we're working from: anything that touches card data, or runs an operating system, must not stay past end-of-life. That covers countertop terminals, mobile readers, PIN pads, and the POS register software itself — if it reads a card or sits on your network, an unpatched one is a liability, full stop. Anything else is judged case by case in the assessment. A cash drawer or receipt printer that never touches card data may be fine to keep running well past its official retirement — but only once Mike has confirmed exactly what role it plays in your setup. Nothing here is a blanket pass; the draft label exists because the safe call depends on how each piece is actually connected. Redundancy The spare-terminal audit Most end-of-life pain isn't the failure — it's the lead time. If your terminal dies and the replacement takes five business days, that's five days of cash-only. The assessment checks whether you have a working spare on hand — and whether it's the right kind for how you actually take payments (a countertop spare doesn't help a mobile setup). One spare terminal is the cheapest business-interruption insurance in the building. The end-of-life assessment runs as part of the POS health check above. Run one day's close and make sure every tender type on the report matches how the money actually arrived. 2 Missing tip prompts If the terminal skips the tip screen, that's gratuity your staff never sees. Check that tip prompts appear on every terminal — countertop and mobile — for each tender type where they belong. 3 Unreconciled batches Batches that never settle never get paid. Sector overview Why grocery POS is its own discipline. Grocery is the highest-transaction, lowest-margin corner of retail. A lane that stalls for thirty seconds creates a line; a deli scale that drifts creates shrink; a PLU file that's out of date creates wrong prices at the shelf edge and at the till. Everything in this sector is about throughput and accuracy at the same time — and the equipment choices follow from that. What makes grocery different from general retail: Weighed items. Deli, produce, and bulk goods are priced by weight. The scale and label printer must talk to the POS so a weight-embedded barcode scans like any other item — and the scale needs regular accuracy checks. PLU codes. When a barcode won't scan (or the item has none), cashiers fall back to price-lookup codes. A printed PLU backup at the lane keeps things moving when the system doesn't. Perishables and shrink. Spoilage, damage, and markdowns eat margin daily. Inventory and receiving discipline matters more here than in any other sector on this site. Direct-store-delivery (DSD) vendors. Bread, dairy, and beverage vendors stock your shelves directly. Receiving has to reconcile what they say they delivered with what actually arrived. Age-restricted items. Tobacco, lottery, and in some provinces alcohol need age-verification prompts configured at the POS — get this wrong and it's a compliance problem, not just a training one. On payments specifically: grocery sees a heavy debit mix (in Canada, Interac), high transaction counts, and small average tickets. That makes your per-transaction fees disproportionately important — a pricing plan that looks fine on percentage rate alone can be expensive once flat per-tap fees multiply across thousands of small baskets. This is exactly what a statement audit catches. 2. In-store hardware & software The roles each piece plays across the lanes and the back office. 🧾 Lane POS station The cashier's screen and computer at each checkout lane. Wired via Ethernet — lanes are the last place you want a Wi-Fi hiccup mid-transaction. 💳 Lane payment terminal Ethernet-connected (ideally semi-integrated with the POS so amounts flow automatically) card terminal at each lane. Handles the tap/insert/swipe volume all day. 🔫 Presentation scanner Hands-free scanner the cashier slides items across. USB-connected; reads both shelf barcodes and weight-embedded deli labels. 🖨️ Receipt printer USB or Ethernet thermal printer at each lane. The cash drawer usually connects through the printer's drawer-kick port. ⚖️ Deli scale & label printer Weighs deli/produce items and prints weight-embedded barcode labels the lane scanner reads. Uses the wired link your scale vendor supports. 🖥️ Back-office PC Ethernet-connected PC for receiving, inventory, price changes, label printing, and end-of-day reconciliation — away from the lanes. Software side: the POS runs the lanes, inventory/receiving tracks what's on the shelf and what spoiled, the scale/label software manages PLUs and label formats, and accounting/payroll closes the loop. Purchasing ties it together — see the integrations section below. 3. Sample setup: a two-lane independent grocer One workable layout for a small grocery or large convenience store. text: $ FairRate Audit Home How it works POS services Cost simulator Resources About FAQ Contact Search Free audit Sector guide · Hotels & hospitality Hotel payments, explained for hotel people Hotels don't take payments the way shops do: pre-authorizations at check-in, incidental holds, restaurant charges posted to the room, and settlement at checkout. This guide walks through the hardware, the setup, the costs, and the mistakes that quietly eat margin. Request your free audit Explore POS services Home › Resources › Hotels & hospitality I run a: Retail stores Hotels & hospitality Restaurants & cafés Quick-service / café Grocery & convenience Services & salons ← Back to the Resources hub 1. Sector overview Why hotel payments are a different animal from retail checkout. In a shop, a sale is one card tap and it's over. In a hotel, a single guest stay can involve four or five separate money events: a pre-authorization (a temporary hold on the card) at check-in, incremental authorizations if the guest's spending grows during the stay, room charges posted from the restaurant, bar, or spa to the guest's folio, and a final settlement (capturing the actual amount) at checkout. If any link in that chain is misconfigured, money leaks: holds that never release, authorizations that expire before settlement, or folio postings that land on the wrong room. The property management system (PMS) is the hub of everything. Reservations, room assignments, folios, and the night audit all live there — and the payment terminals talk to the PMS through a payment interface rather than acting as standalone checkout devices. That makes compatibility between your terminals, your processor, and your PMS vendor the single most important purchasing decision. A terminal that works beautifully in a retail store can be the wrong device for a front desk if your PMS vendor doesn't support it. Two more hotel-specific realities shape every decision in this guide: Guests bring their own network expectations. Your property runs guest Wi-Fi, and that traffic must never share a network with payments, the PMS, or the outlet POS. Segmentation isn't optional — it's the difference between a contained network and a breach that touches every system. Payment costs sit outside your IT budget. Processing fees rarely appear in formal technology spending figures, which is why two hotels with identical tech stacks can have wildly different total costs. Any honest cost comparison has to include processing. ⚠️ Confirm terminal compatibility with your PMS vendor first Before you change processors, buy terminals, or sign anything: ask your PMS vendor which payment terminals and processors their payment interface supports. An incompatible terminal means the pre-authorization and folio-settlement flow above simply won't work — and you'll discover it at the worst possible moment. Get the answer in writing , and while you're at it, confirm token portability (whether card tokens move with you if you change processors later) in writing too. 2. In-store hardware & software The roles each piece of equipment plays at the front desk and across the property. 🖥️ Front-desk workstation The PC or terminal the front-desk team uses to run the PMS. Wired via Ethernet for reliability — this is not the device to put on Wi-Fi. 💳 Countertop payment terminals Ethernet-connected terminals at the desk that talk to the PMS through the payment interface. These handle pre-authorizations, incremental authorizations, and checkout settlement. 📱 Mobile payment terminal For the pool bar, valet, room service, or anywhere away from the desk. Runs over cellular or the property's operational Wi-Fi — never guest Wi-Fi. 🔌 Payment interface service Software (usually on your property LAN) that connects the PMS to the payment terminals and the processor. If this goes down, the desk can't take cards — even if the terminals look fine. 🍽️ Outlet POS The restaurant, bar, café, or spa POS. It posts charges to the guest's room folio in the PMS rather than settling them independently — that's what makes it hotel POS rather than restaurant POS. 🖨️ Receipt printer & cash drawer Folio receipts at checkout and a drawer for the cash that still moves at most front desks. The drawer typically connects through the printer's cash-drawer port. On the software side, the stack is: PMS (system of record) → payment interface (connects PMS to processor) → processor (moves the money). Around that orbit the booking engine on your website, the channel manager that syncs rates and availability to online travel agencies, and accounting software that receives summarized revenue from the night audit. 3. Sector overview Retail covers independent shops and specialty stores — apparel, gifts, electronics, hobby, home goods, and similar single- or few-location businesses. What makes retail different from other sectors: Inventory is the business. SKUs, variants (size/colour), suppliers, purchase orders, stock counts, and shrink drive almost every POS decision. Checkout is lane-based. One or more fixed lanes, each with a POS station, payment terminal, printer, drawer, and often a barcode scanner. Multi-channel is normal. Many shops sell in-store and online; the two stock pools must stay in sync or you oversell. Debit matters in Canada. Holiday rushes stress lanes, returns, and stock counts — your setup should be tested before December, not during it. 2. In-store hardware & software Think in roles and connection types , not brand names. If you can describe each role, you can compare any vendor honestly. text: $ FairRate Audit Home How it works POS services Cost simulator Resources About FAQ Contact Search Free audit Sector guide · Services & salons Salon payments: bookings, no-shows, and card-on-file done right Salons, spas, barbershops, and appointment businesses live or die on the calendar: deposits, no-show policies, tips, retail product sales, and gift cards. Sector overview Why appointment businesses need different payment thinking. A salon's money problems are calendar problems. The booking fills the chair; the payment has to follow without friction, whether that's a deposit at booking time, full payment at the chair, a no-show charge under a stated policy, or a tip added after the service. Every one of those flows touches card-on-file — and card-on-file done wrong is both a compliance risk and a customer-trust risk. What makes this sector different: Card-on-file and tokens. Deposits and no-show charges require storing a reusable payment reference — a token , never the raw card number. Tokens live in your processor's vault; your booking platform references them. Ask about token portability before you change processors, or switching becomes a project. No-show and late-cancellation policies. Charging a no-show fee is only defensible (and only worth the dispute risk) with a clear, stated policy the client agreed to at booking. Tips. Tip prompts at checkout need to be present but not pushy — and tip handling has payroll implications for commission-based staff. Retail product sales. Shampoo, styling products, and gift sets sold at the front desk are ordinary retail checkout — barcodes, inventory, and all. Gift cards. A meaningful revenue line for salons, and a liability until redeemed. Your system has to track balances honestly. ⚠️ Never store raw card numbers Card capture must be tokenized : the card number goes to the processor's vault, and your systems keep only a token reference. If any part of your setup — a spreadsheet, a booking note field, an old terminal — holds actual card numbers, that's a PCI scope and breach-risk problem. See the PCI scope guide for the conceptual picture. 2. In-store hardware & software A salon counter needs less hardware than a grocery lane — but the software connections matter more. 💳 Front-desk payment terminal The countertop terminal for in-person checkout: services, tips, and retail products. Ethernet or reliable Wi-Fi — pick the one your space actually supports. 📋 Booking tablet / workstation Runs the booking calendar: appointments, client records, reminders, and deposits. Often a tablet at the desk or a back-office PC. 🖨️ Receipt printer (optional) Thermal printer for clients who want a paper receipt. Many salons go email/SMS receipts only — a legitimate choice if your clientele prefers it. Software side: the cloud booking platform is the operational hub (calendar, reminders, client records, gift cards, marketing). The processor's token vault holds the card tokens. The payment terminal bridges in-person checkout. Accounting and payroll/commissions close the loop. The critical rule: card data flows to the token vault, never into the booking platform's own database as raw numbers. 3. Put the terminal where the client can comfortably see the tip prompt and tap — not behind the desk where staff have to hand it over. If the terminal is on Wi-Fi, use your business network, never a guest network clients join. Keep a charger at the desk if any device is a tablet — a dead booking screen at 9am ruins the day. Daily workflow Opening: terminal charged and connected; booking calendar loaded and today's appointments confirmed. Before appointments: automated reminders go out (your booking platform handles this — verify they're actually sending). Checkout: in-person terminal payment, or a tokenized card-on-file charge for deposits and pre-paids. Do not make operational changes in anticipation. Sources: EPOS Now · Morningstar · IntelliPay Free tool · settlement math The flat-rate settlement trap Headlines say interchange is getting cheaper. But whether you see any of that depends entirely on how your processor prices you — and for most small businesses on bundled flat-rate plans, the answer is: you won't. Not automatically. How the pass-through actually works 1 Interchange is the wholesale cost The card networks set interchange — the biggest slice of every card transaction's cost. Your processor adds its own markup on top. This is true for every plan, no matter how it's priced. 2 Flat-rate = bundled A flat-rate processor charges one bundled percentage regardless of the underlying interchange. When wholesale interchange drops, your rate doesn't move — the difference widens your processor's margin, not your savings. 3 Interchange-plus = transparent On interchange-plus, wholesale interchange passes through at cost with a fixed processor markup beside it. An interchange cut flows to you automatically, line by line, on your next statement. That's the whole trap: the settlement lowers the wholesale cost. Only merchants whose pricing passes wholesale costs through will see it. Everyone else's processor keeps it — quietly, on every transaction, for five years. This is a general mechanic of bundled pricing, true of any flat-rate plan. And a reminder: the settlement isn't final, so treat the numbers below as what would happen, not what will. One rate, one line, done. The simplicity is the point — and the trap. You're on interchange-plus if… Your statement itemizes interchange categories (standard, premium, commercial, foreign…) at their individual rates, with a separate processor markup line — often a small basis-point fee plus a per-transaction fee.
